Getting started: CATE and regression

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

This walkthrough fits conditional average treatment effects (CATE) and conditional means at selected covariate profiles. Install the package using the README. Use browseVignettes("RdistNN") to open the installed guide collection. The paper gives the statistical assumptions and results; this guide covers the calls and how to read their outputs.

Use x0 for one profile or X0 for a matrix with one profile per row. Covariates and supplied predictions must be finite, complete and aligned in the same observation order. Data-frame targets follow the x_cols order.

Conditional average treatment effects

For binary treatment D, the AIPW inputs are outcome Y, control and treated conditional means m0 and m1, and propensity e. Nuisance fitting is external to the package. This simulation supplies oracle nuisances so that the example demonstrates localization without choosing a nuisance learner.

demo_cate <- cate_demo_data(n = 180, p = 2, design = "hetero", seed = 1)
df <- demo_cate$data

fit_cate <- cate_dnn(
  data = df, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y", t_col = "D",
  m0_col = "m0_oracle", m1_col = "m1_oracle", e_col = "e_oracle",
  x0 = c(0, 0), k = 1L, se = TRUE,
  return = c("W", "dx")
)

summary(fit_cate)
#> <summary.cate_result>
#>   signal: aipw
#>   localization: s = 19, s/n = 0.106
#>   targets: 1
#>          estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
#> target_1   0.4527    0.2607     1.737 0.08242 -0.05817    0.9636
confint(fit_cate)
#>             conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -0.05817257 0.9636003
predict(fit_cate, x0 = c(0.2, -0.1), interval = "confidence")
#>            fit       lwr      upr
#> [1,] 0.7890503 0.4451826 1.132918

fit_cate$tau contains the estimates and fit_cate$se contains their jackknife standard errors. nobs(fit_cate) counts training observations; local effective sample size describes weight concentration. confint() returns pointwise normal intervals, not simultaneous confidence bands.

If you already have an observation-level pseudo-outcome, pass it directly. Here we use the aligned oracle AIPW column from the same demo data:

X <- as.matrix(df[c("X1", "X2")])
fit_cate_matrix <- cate_dnn(
  X = X, x0 = c(0, 0), pseudo_outcome = df$aipw_oracle, k = 1L
)

c(data_frame = fit_cate$tau, matrix = fit_cate_matrix$tau)
#> data_frame     matrix 
#>  0.4527139  0.4527139

The data-frame pathway also accepts pseudo_outcome. See ?cate_dnn for the complete input contract. Preserve the same observation order for every nuisance or pseudo-outcome vector.

Migrating earlier CATE inputs

The normalized Robinson construction has been removed. Replace earlier m_col calls with propensity and both arm-specific outcome means for AIPW, or supply an externally justified signal through pseudo_outcome. A pooled outcome mean is not a substitute for the two arm means. Demo data now include m1_oracle and aipw_oracle; the former rho_oracle used a different signal, so this is not a numerically equivalent column rename.

Fresh nuisance-based fitting constructs mu1 - mu0 + D*(Y-mu1)/e - (1-D)*(Y-mu0)/(1-e), with validated and clipped propensities. The retired m_col argument remains rejected. A directly supplied pseudo_outcome takes precedence over accompanying nuisance selectors and is localized unchanged; its construction, causal interpretation and inferential justification remain the caller’s responsibility. The paper’s residualized-slope estimating equation is distinct from the removed normalized pseudo-outcome.

Each new fit records meta$signal_source: "aipw" means the package constructed the signal through its nuisance-input branch, and "supplied" means the caller provided it. A supplied vector remains "supplied" even when it equals AIPW or comes from a column named aipw_oracle. meta$created_with_version records the version of the package actually loaded when the original fit was created. Candidate views and summaries preserve that version. Neither field certifies identification, same-sample nuisance accuracy or stability, localization bias, or the conditions for pointwise inference.

Refit objects created by older development versions. Both packages reuse current fitted state for prediction, covariance, candidates and diagnostics; they do not reconstruct retired object schemas or score methods. Prediction returns ordinary numeric vectors, matrices or list(fit, se.fit). See the companion’s saved-fit guide.

Covariance between prespecified profiles 

profiles <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.2, -0.1))
joint <- cate_dnn(X = X, X0 = profiles, pseudo_outcome = df$aipw_oracle,
                 s = fit_cate$meta$s, return = character())
V <- vcov(joint)
a <- c(1, -1)
c(contrast = sum(a * coef(joint)),
  contrast_se = sqrt(drop(crossprod(a, V %*% a))))
#>    contrast contrast_se 
#>  -0.3363364   0.1739546

Both covariance axes follow coef(joint). Common deleted observations retain dependence between profiles. Valid contrast inference requires the relevant joint assumptions; pointwise intervals alone do not establish it.

The documented sampling framework uses independent observations and supplies neither cluster nor survey-design inference. Exact distance ties use the original covariates lexicographically in their supplied column order. Identical localization covariate rows receive their block’s average weight, with the same rule applied to every deletion’s remaining block. Outcomes, treatments and nuisance values do not define the groups. Aligned row permutations then preserve estimates and covariance up to numerical precision. A warning identifies this practical modification, which is not covered by the paper’s theory. Individual weights, support and ESS can change. The reported s/n is descriptive; it is not a calibrated inference threshold.

Check local support

Supplied propensities must lie in [0, 1]; AIPW uses clipped values with clip = 1e-8 by default. Clipping prevents undefined denominators but cannot create local treatment support. Supplied pseudo-outcomes are used unchanged.

Inspect local weight concentration and treated/control mass:

d_cate <- as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit_cate))
d_cate[, c("target_id", "n_eff", "treated_mass", "control_mass")]
#>          target_id    n_eff treated_mass control_mass
#> target_1  target_1 17.52493    0.7317029    0.2682971

Diagnostics describe the realized sample near a target; they are not a test of the paper’s assumptions. Keep "W" in return for weight diagnostics, "dx" for metric-distance summaries. Overlap remains available from the supplied treatment/propensity inputs without requesting a "nuisance" extra.

Nonparametric regression

np_dnn() estimates a conditional mean. Regression fits support the same summary(), coef(), confint(), vcov(), nobs() and predict() calls as CATE; their direct estimate and standard-error fields are mu and se.

demo_np <- np_demo_data(n = 160, p = 2, design = "sinusoidal", seed = 2)
fit_np <- np_dnn(
  data = demo_np$data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y",
  X0 = rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.5, 0)), k = 1L, se = TRUE,
  return = c("W", "dx", "ess")
)

summary(fit_np)$coefficients
#>             estimate std.error  statistic    p.value    conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -0.08841632 0.1517981 -0.5824601 0.56025679 -0.38593504 0.2091024
#> target_2  0.24768566 0.1328475  1.8644359 0.06226051 -0.01269067 0.5080620
confint(fit_np)
#>             conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -0.38593504 0.2091024
#> target_2 -0.01269067 0.5080620
predict(fit_np, x0 = c(0.2, -0.1), interval = "confidence")
#>             fit       lwr       upr
#> [1,] 0.06621915 -0.250889 0.3833273

Use uppercase Y for the matrix interface:

fit_np_matrix <- np_dnn(
  X = as.matrix(demo_np$data[c("X1", "X2")]),
  Y = demo_np$data$Y, x0 = c(0, 0), k = 1L
)
fit_np_matrix$mu
#> [1] -0.08841632

predict() evaluates new profiles using the retained training outcomes and geometry. Two-scale regression uses np_tdnn() with orders s1 < s2 and s2 < n for jackknife uncertainty. See ?np_tdnn for its signed weights and additional requirements.

Choosing localization and uncertainty settings

The defaults use exact DNN weights and k = 1. Unless s or tuning is supplied, the subsample order is s = floor(0.4 * n^((p + 1)/(p + 2))), where p is the covariate dimension. Larger s concentrates more weight near the target. The written manuscript derivations use k = 1; larger fixed k is supported in the implementation.

The order s is not a count of observations retained in a nearest-neighbor truncation. The unaveraged exact rank table has support through rank n - s + k (n - s + 1 for k = 1). Block averaging can extend nonzero observation weights to the end of an identical-covariate block crossing that edge. The optional neighbors extra reports the first k neighbors, rather than the full weight support.

For sensitivity analysis, compare the paper’s candidate orders without changing the primary result:

fit_grid <- np_dnn(
  data = demo_np$data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y",
  x0 = c(0, 0), tuning_mode = "grid", se = FALSE
)
fit_grid$tuning_grid$candidates
#>   candidate_id computed_key is_default feasible reason status lambda  s
#> 1   lambda_0p3         s_13      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.30 13
#> 2   lambda_0p4         s_17       TRUE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.40 17
#> 3   lambda_0p5         s_22      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.50 22
#> 4  lambda_0p75         s_33      FALSE     TRUE     ok     ok   0.75 33
candidate_fit(fit_grid, 1L)$mu
#> [1] -0.0286826

tuning_dnn_paper() uses lambda = 0.4 and the grid c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.75); s is recomputed for each candidate. Grid mode is a sensitivity comparison, not an automatic optimization rule. It cannot be combined with explicit s.

For uncertainty, jackknife = "fast" reuses full-sample ranks; jackknife = "loo" directly recomputes leave-one-out weights. Delete-1 inference requires s < n. Set se = FALSE to omit standard errors.

Seeds and native threads

The demo helpers’ explicit seed arguments restore the caller’s saved RNG state. seed = NULL draws from the current stream. Simulation grids use master_seed to generate their replicate seeds. To reproduce a grid, also retain the RNG kind, dependency versions and availability, future plan and tuning configuration; equal integer seeds alone do not guarantee agreement between the future.apply route and its fallback. See ?sim_cate_run for the reproducibility contract shared with sim_iv_run().

Native routines default to at most two OpenMP threads. Set options(RdistNN.num_threads = 4L) to request four, or 1L for one native thread. Lower OpenMP runtime limits still apply. See ?RdistNN for the controls and saved-RNG-state limitations.

Plots and reusable weights

Plotting is optional and requires ggplot2. Dashboards additionally require patchwork. Both fitted workflows support the estimate and weight views:

plot(fit_np)

plot_weights(fit_cate, type = "profile")

For your own scalar signal, build weights directly. Rows of W index observations and columns index target points:

wt <- weights_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.5, 0)), k = 1L, s = 12L,
  return = "W"
)
dim(wt$W)
#> [1] 180   2
as.vector(crossprod(wt$W, fit_cate$psi))
#> [1] 0.03588061 0.01509280 0.01509280 0.03588061
